headline: High-risk shared git/workspace interaction and broad egress create leakage and conflict; RD-Agent’s API-driven outputs can cascade into Aider edits.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Aider reads and writes repo files and shares state via a git repo, while RD-Agent can produce logs, traces, and files that Aider may ingest as trusted content. No direct shared clipboard/MCP channel is shown, so this is not high, but the shared workspace makes instruction smuggling plausible.
conditions: IF RD-Agent writes attacker-controlled text into repo-tracked files or logs that Aider later reads as instructions, injection is possible.
IF the two agents are pointed at the same repository workspace, shared-file prompt injection becomes reachable.
mitigations: Separate the agents into different repos or directories.
Add a human review step before Aider consumes RD-Agent-generated files.
Strip or quarantine logs and traces before Aider reads them.
Use read-only mounts for RD-Agent outputs where possible.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for machine-generated files.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Aider touches source code and git history and has broad network egress; RD-Agent touches financial reports, papers, datasets, execution traces, and logs and also has broad egress. If they share a workspace, sensitive artifacts can move from one agent into the other’s outputs or API calls. The profiles do not prove a shared OS account, so medium fits.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same workspace, files from RD-Agent can be exposed to Aider.
IF either agent forwards file contents to its model provider, sensitive code, reports, or traces may leave the local environment.
mitigations: Keep separate workspaces and separate credentials.
Disable access to sensitive datasets in the shared repo.
Review outbound prompts for file attachments before execution.
Rotate any exposed API keys immediately after a shared run.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent data-loss-prevention filters.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Aider can execute shell commands, write the filesystem, and modify git state; RD-Agent can run browsers and call multiple APIs, with both supporting multiple instances. Because Aider explicitly shares state via a git repo and neither profile shows locking, concurrent writes to the same repo can corrupt work or overwrite commits. Uncertainty favors the higher severity.
conditions: IF both agents target the same git repository, concurrent edits can race.
IF RD-Agent writes artifacts while Aider commits changes, git history conflicts can occur without locking.
mitigations: Run the agents in separate clones.
Serialize all git writes through one operator.
Disable automatic commits for one agent during overlap.
Use branch-per-agent workflows.
requires-engineering: add repository locking or transactional merge orchestration.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Aider is an editing agent that can act on text it receives, while RD-Agent is a research/automation agent that produces papers, traces, logs, and API-backed outputs. If RD-Agent’s outputs are fed into Aider without verification, Aider may turn incorrect research artifacts into code or commits. The profiles do not show a mandatory verification gate, so the pathway exists in default use.
conditions: IF RD-Agent output is used as authoritative input to Aider, errors can propagate into commits.
IF Aider is allowed to edit code based on unreviewed RD-Agent summaries, cascading mistakes become likely.
mitigations: Require human review before Aider acts on RD-Agent output.
Compare RD-Agent claims against source artifacts before editing.
Limit Aider to draft-only mode for RD-Agent-derived tasks.
Keep a changelog of source-to-edit mappings.
requires-engineering: add automated verification between research output and code edits.

E_compliance.rationale: RD-Agent explicitly touches financial reports, competition datasets, execution traces, and logs and uses third-party APIs such as OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, DeepSeek, and Kaggle. Aider handles source code and git history and also sends prompts to configured model providers. If regulated or confidential data is placed into either agent, the pair can move it to external services without a documented residency or retention control here, so compliance risk is high.
conditions: IF regulated data such as financial reports or confidential code is processed through either agent, external API transfer may violate policy.
IF the deployment requires strict retention or residency controls, neither profile documents them here.
mitigations: Restrict both agents to non-sensitive data.
Disable external API providers for regulated workloads.
Confirm data-processing agreements before use.
Purge logs after each run.
requires-engineering: implement residency and retention enforcement per agent.
